newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Assembly adopts private pensions bill.
newsitem.headline: French Assembly adopts private pensions bill.

text.p: France's National Assembly adopted a bill on Wednesday to allow creation of private pension funds, ignoring trade union warnings that the legislation could run down the existing state-backed retirement benefit system.

President Jacques Chirac said the bill was not a threat to the current pension system, which is under increasing strain as the number of pensioners outpaces those who work and pay social security contributions.

"The (current) distribution system is the foundation of our retirements. We are not considering questioning them and I am their guarantor," Chirac was quoted as saying by government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.

The legislation, which will give about 14 million private sector employees the option to save for their own retirement, was voted on after a second reading by just 47 of the assembly's 577 members, with 34 in favour and 13 against.
The poor turnout was blamed on a long and raucous debate which dragged late into Tuesday night amid resistance from opposition Socialist and Communist parliamentarians.

The legislation must now return for a second reading in the Senate, or upper house, on January 30. It will also have to go through joint consultation between the two houses of parliament if the Senate introduces any modifications.

While some unions are not ideologically opposed, four of the country's leading unions joined forces on Monday to condemn the bill because it would deprive the current system of vital funds by exempting employers paying into private funds from social security charges on those contributions.

The bill offers tax relief to companies and employees who subscribe to private funds, which amounts to people saving for their own pensions on top of relying on a current system where those in work pay for those in retirement.

The private pensions bill is also designed to boost the stock market by capping the amount private pension funds can put into government bonds at 65 percent. This ensures at least 35 percent goes into equities without breaching European Union laws prohibiting the setting of minimum limits for equity investment.

Unions fear tax relief and exemption from social security charges will siphon off money that would otherwise have gone into the existing "distribution" system, made up of the basic social security pension and the top-up ARRCO and AGIRC schemes.
On Monday the unions put the potential loss to the social security system in a year at 18 billion francs ($3.3 billion).

This was dismissed by the bill's author, Jean-Pierre Thomas, who said the existing basic and top-up regimes would forego about 2.1 billion francs at most, out of some 700 billion francs under their management.

They also argue that the new system will encourage employers to offer to contribute to private pensions rather than award pay rises because the latter would be subject to the full weight of social security levies.
The new funds will be set up under voluntary agreements between companies and their employees or at the level of an industry or profession.
The plans are part of an overall tax reform designed to funnel French savings into productive investment with the aim of fuelling growth and helping to bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment.
The government has also said, however, that it does not intend to raise taxation on savings and a stable environment supportive of investment was needed. ($1=5.395 French Franc)
